title: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
summary: How Miles extends slime's SGLang plus Megatron loop: Python launchers, fully async RL, TITO, environment connectors, MoE routing replay, precision contracts, P2P weight sync, LoRA and multi-LoRA.
outcomes: Launch a Miles recipe, override it with --extra-args, and read its metrics against the monitoring table
Explain how fully async rollout keeps engines busy and compute a group's staleness from its weight versions
Explain why retokenization and MoE routing flips corrupt RL gradients and how TITO and R3 remove them
Choose which rollout layer an environment or connector replaces, and what always stays in Miles
Compare TIS, clip-or-pop, sampling-support replay and true-on-policy alignment as answers to rollout and trainer mismatch
Explain the precision contract and which rollout and trainer formats may be paired
Choose between broadcast, P2P RDMA and disk-delta weight transfer from fleet size and topology
Compute LoRA's weight-sync saving and explain versioned adapters in the multi-LoRA service

lessons.title: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale

blocks.md:
You already know slime: SGLang engines generate rollouts, Megatron-LM trains, and new weights flow back to the engines every step. **Miles** is RadixArk's RL post-training framework, and its README states plainly that it was *forked from slime*. Its technical report says Miles "builds on the clean design of slime" and organizes everything around one principle: components should be *verified, clean, and customizable*.

The report frames frontier RL as two problems. **Throughput**: rollouts are now multi-turn, tool-using episodes on trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, so hardware sits idle while the slowest trajectory finishes. **Fidelity**: the numbers the trainer computes can silently diverge from what the policy actually sampled, which corrupts the gradient without raising any error.

Four terms recur in this course, all defined in the report. A **prompt** is one task from the dataset. A **trajectory** is one attempt at it; for agentic work, a whole multi-turn episode with tool calls and environment replies. A **group** is the set of trajectories for the same prompt; GRPO (group relative policy optimization), which you met in the GRPO course and ran in slime, scores each trajectory against its siblings: its advantage is its reward minus the group's mean reward, divided by the group's standard deviation, so Miles schedules, buffers and discards data one group at a time. A **session** is what the serving layer sees: the ordered requests of one episode.

blocks.title: The Miles RL loop and where its additions attach

scenes.caption: Rollout: prompts go through the SGLang router to the engines, which generate trajectories (one attempt at a prompt) in groups that share a prompt.
Scoring: in agentic RL each trajectory acts in its own environment, which executes tool calls and returns a reward.
Training: finished groups go to a buffer, and the trainer consumes a batch of them, computes the RL loss and steps the optimizer.
Weight update: new weights go back to the engines so the next trajectories come from the updated policy. This closes the loop that slime also runs.

Where Miles adds machinery: async buffer with staleness control, TITO (lesson 4) and R3 (lesson 6) on the rollout side, the low-precision contract in the trainer (lesson 7), P2P transfer on the update edge, engine recovery.

blocks.md: The loop has one bookkeeping rule from the Core Concepts docs. Two knobs set how much rollout produces, two set how much training consumes, and they must agree, so every sample generated is trained on exactly once. Set three and Miles fills in the fourth; set all four inconsistently and Miles aborts with a validation error.

blocks.caption: The four-knob invariant from the Miles Core Concepts page.

blocks.prompt: A launch script sets 32 prompts per rollout, 8 samples per prompt and a global batch of 64 samples. How many optimizer steps does each rollout feed?
blocks.reveal: $32 \times 8 = 256$ samples per rollout, and $256 / 64 = 4$. So `num_steps_per_rollout` is 4. Set it to 3 and Miles refuses to start rather than silently dropping or reusing 64 samples.

blocks.md:
Around this loop Miles offers choices that are swappable behind small interfaces:

- **Training backend** (`--train-backend`): `megatron` (the default, with the TP, PP, CP (context parallelism) and EP you met in slime, plus ETP, expert tensor parallelism, which splits each expert's own weight matrices across GPUs the way TP splits a dense layer), `fsdp` (fully sharded data parallel: every GPU keeps only a slice of each layer's parameters, gradients and optimizer state, and all-gathers a layer's full parameters just before using it; Miles runs the model's own Hugging Face code under FSDP2, PyTorch's second implementation of it, loaded as-is), or `torchtitan` (PyTorch's own reference library for large-scale training, whose trainer Miles drives as a black box).

The **cluster backend** is Ray by default, or Kubernetes, where the run installs as a Helm release (Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes, and a release is one installed copy of a package) and its worker pools are LeaderWorkerSets (a Kubernetes resource that starts a group of pods as one unit, a leader plus its workers, for jobs that span several hosts). The docs mark the Kubernetes path as under active development.

The third choice is the **algorithm**: `--advantage-estimator` (the rule that turns rewards into each token's advantage) accepts `grpo` (default); `gspo` (GSPO: one importance ratio per response); `reinforce_plus_plus` (REINFORCE++: no value model; the reward sits on the last token, a KL penalty with coefficient `--kl-coef` on every token, and returns summed backward with discount `--gamma`, default 1); `reinforce_plus_plus_baseline` (the group-mean-centered reward minus the per-token KL penalty); and `ppo` (a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation). The slime lesson "The trainer side: from scored samples to a policy-gradient step" works through these; Miles has the same set except slime's `cispo`. Two details. Batch-wide whitening is a separate switch, `--normalize-advantages`, off by default, but Miles refuses to start either REINFORCE++ estimator without it. On-policy distillation (lesson 9) edits advantages after the estimator runs and before that whitening, so it composes with any of them. SFT (supervised fine-tuning) reuses the same trainer with no rollout engine.

Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).
The Miles docs do not publish a line-by-line diff against slime. This course teaches what Miles documents and measures; do not conclude from it that slime lacks any particular feature.

The report's word **verified** has a concrete meaning in Miles's CI. Nightly and weekly CI runs write each gated test's training metrics into Miles's own database, and every run's new numbers are judged against that history, so a slow drift that no single run would reveal fails the build once a coordinate has 10 trusted values; below that a failing check is only reported. A number is compared only with earlier numbers of the same kind. The run series is (test, backend, suite), where the suite is the GPU stage the run actually executed on, so Blackwell numbers never regress against Hopper ones. Inside a run the coordinate is (metric, step): step-0 `train/ppo_kl` is compared only with past step-0 `ppo_kl`, never with step 1 or with `grad_norm`. The reference is the mean of that coordinate's trusted past values; with no trusted values yet the gate is inactive, which is how a new baseline seeds itself.

blocks.caption: The band for one coordinate: r is a relative band, f an absolute floor. Both scale from the reference, so a deviating value cannot widen its own tolerance. For train/ppo_kl the defaults are r up 0.5, f up 0.02, r down 0.8, f down 0.02; rollout/raw_reward has no upper bound.

blocks.code:
# evaluate_constraint from tests/ci/metric_history/constraints.py (Miles main), run on CPU
history = [0.010, 0.012, 0.011]   # trusted step-0 train/ppo_kl values (illustrative)
ref = sum(history) / len(history)
rule = {"rel_up": 0.5, "abs_floor_up": 0.02, "rel_down": 0.8, "abs_floor_down": 0.02}
for cur in (0.013, 0.045):
    o = evaluate_constraint(rule, cur, ref)
    print(f"ref {ref:.4f}  cur {cur:.3f}  corridor [{o.lo:.4f}, {o.hi:.4f}]  pass {o.ok}")

# ref 0.0110  cur 0.013  corridor [-0.0090, 0.0310]  pass True
# ref 0.0110  cur 0.045  corridor [-0.0090, 0.0310]  pass False
blocks.caption: Near zero the absolute floor dominates: 0.5 x 0.011 is only 0.0055, so the 0.02 floor sets the upper band.

blocks.prompt: A pull request changes a kernel, and the CI run's step-0 train/ppo_kl comes out at 0.045 while step 1 matches history. The step-1 history for ppo_kl averages 0.05. Does the gate pass?
blocks.reveal: No. Step 0 is judged only against step-0 history (mean 0.011), whose corridor tops out at $0.011 + \max(0.5 \times 0.011, 0.02) = 0.031$. That step 1 is normally around 0.05 is irrelevant: it is a different coordinate. At step 0 nothing has been updated yet, so a jump there points at the change, which is exactly what the gate is for.

blocks.question: You need to post-train a 700B-parameter MoE whose training job spans several racks and needs expert parallelism. Which training backend do the Miles docs point you to?
options: Megatron-LM, the default and the backend for 100B+ MoE models that need model parallelism
FSDP, because it loads the Hugging Face checkpoint with no conversion
torchtitan, because it is driven as a black box
Any of them; the backend only changes checkpoint format
blocks.explain: The training-backend page says to use Megatron-LM for large models and anything that needs real parallelism, such as a 100B+ MoE or a job spanning racks. FSDP is the fast path for new architectures and models that fit under data parallelism alone. The backend changes how the model is split, not only its checkpoints.

blocks.question: A colleague sets rollout_batch_size 16, n_samples_per_prompt 4, global_batch_size 32 and num_steps_per_rollout 3. What happens?
options: Miles trains 3 steps and discards the 16 unused samples
Miles aborts with a validation error because 64 is not equal to 96
Miles reuses 32 samples to fill the third step
Miles silently changes n_samples_per_prompt to 6
blocks.explain: 16 x 4 = 64 samples are produced, but 32 x 3 = 96 would be consumed. With all four knobs set inconsistently, the docs say Miles aborts with a validation error instead of guessing which knob you meant.

lessons.title: Launching and watching a Miles run

blocks.md:
In slime you start a run with a shell script that fills bash arrays and calls `ray job submit`. In Miles the quick start is one Python command:

`python scripts/run_qwen3_dense.py --model-name Qwen3-4B`

Before it, the quick start pulls the `radixark/miles` container on an 8-GPU node, downloads Qwen3-4B, the dapo-math-17k training prompts and the AIME-2024 set (evaluated on, never trained on), and converts the Hugging Face weights once into Megatron's sharded `torch_dist` format. The Hugging Face directory stays, because the SGLang rollout engines read it.

That command is a **recipe**, not the training process. A launch script assembles the full `train.py` command line for one model family, starts a local Ray cluster and submits the command as a Ray job. Four layers are involved:

- `scripts/run_*.py`, the launch script: per-model values and blocks of flags.
- `scripts/models/<type>.py`: the Megatron architecture flags (layer count, hidden size), because Megatron cannot read the architecture from a Hugging Face checkpoint.
- `command_utils`: starts Ray and submits the job.
- `train.py` or `train_async.py`: the real training process, running inside the Ray job.

The script prints its resolved options as a table, then every shell command it runs with an `EXEC:` prefix, so the log is a complete record of what ran.

blocks.title: What one launch command does

nodes.label:
execute_train
ray start, ray job submit

scenes.caption: The command line and MILES_SCRIPT_* env vars fill the script's own options. A command-line value beats the env var, which beats the field default.
--model-name picks a row of _RECIPES. For Qwen3-4B: TP 2, 9216 tokens per GPU, 2-GPU SGLang engines, memory fraction 0.7, no optimizer offload, 3000 rollouts.
execute() builds one f-string block per concern (checkpoints, rollout, eval, parallelism, GRPO, optimizer, SGLang, misc) and appends --extra-args at the very end.
execute_train kills leftover sglang, miles and redis processes, starts Ray, splices the architecture flags ahead of the recipe flags and submits train.py as a Ray job.
Everything left of the submit runs in the head-node shell and is logged as EXEC: lines; the training itself happens only in train.py.

blocks.md:
The script's own options are the fields of a `ScriptArgs` dataclass, each exposed twice: as a `--kebab-case` flag and as an environment variable with the `MILES_SCRIPT_` prefix (`--model-dir` and `MILES_SCRIPT_MODEL_DIR`). The env form is how cluster tooling injects machine-specific paths without editing the script. Shared options include `--model-dir`, `--data-dir`, `--output-dir`, `--num-nodes`, `--num-gpus-per-node`, `--extra-args` and `--extra-env-vars`.

There are three ways to override a recipe, lightest first:

1. `--extra-args "..."` appends flags to the end of the `train.py` command line, and for a flag given twice the later occurrence wins.
2. Set a `ScriptArgs` option, as a flag or an env var.
3. Edit the script. The docs call it the canonical home of a recipe's hyperparameters, meant to be read and edited.

blocks.prompt: The Qwen3-4B recipe already passes `--lr 1e-6` and `--num-rollout 3000` to train.py. You launch it with `--extra-args "--lr 2e-6 --num-rollout 100"`. Which learning rate and rollout count does train.py use?
blocks.reveal: Both of yours: `2e-6` and `100`. `--extra-args` is appended after every recipe block, so train.py sees each flag twice and, as with any argparse store flag, keeps the last value. Miles's own launcher reads flags the same way (`ArgvManipulator.get_effective` returns the last value). The code below runs the real recipe with the Ray submission stubbed out and shows the argv it builds.

blocks.code:
# run scripts/run_qwen3_dense.py on CPU with the Ray backend stubbed out
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("recipe", "scripts/run_qwen3_dense.py")
recipe = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(recipe)
captured = {}
class StubBackend:
    def execute_train(self, train_args, **kw):
        captured["argv"], captured["kw"] = shlex.split(train_args), kw
recipe.ScriptArgs.create_backend = lambda self: StubBackend()

os.environ["MILES_SCRIPT_MODEL_DIR"] = "/mnt/models"
app = typer.Typer(); app.command()(recipe.main)
typer.main.get_command(app)(standalone_mode=False, args=["--model-name", "Qwen3-4B",
    "--extra-args", "--lr 2e-6 --num-rollout 100"])
argv = captured["argv"]
for f in ["--lr", "--num-rollout", "--hf-checkpoint"]:
    print(f, ArgvManipulator.get(argv, f), ArgvManipulator.get_effective(argv, f))
print(captured["kw"]["megatron_model_type"], len(argv))

# --lr ['1e-6', '2e-6'] 2e-6
# --num-rollout ['3000', '100'] 100
# --hf-checkpoint ['/mnt/models/Qwen3-4B'] /mnt/models/Qwen3-4B
# qwen3-4B 114
blocks.caption: Imports (os, shlex, importlib.util, typer, ArgvManipulator from miles.utils.external_utils.command_utils.common) omitted. Run against Miles main at commit 0989f48 on a Mac CPU: no GPU and no Ray cluster needed.

blocks.md: Architecture flags are not self-validating. Two checkpoints of one family can ship a different `--rotary-base`, vocab padding or norm epsilon. Diff the checkpoint's `config.json` against its file in `scripts/models/` before a first run and append any drifted value, for example `--extra-args "--rotary-base 10000"`.

Once the engines warm up, each rollout prints metric lines, and with `WANDB_API_KEY` exported the launcher adds the wandb flags by itself. Metrics live under `train/`, `rollout/`, `perf/`, `multi_turn/` and `passrate/`. The slime lesson "Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery" gives the order to check things in (responses, reward and log probs, mismatch, staleness). Miles's monitoring page adds a table of healthy and red-flag patterns:

- `loss`: slow decay over hundreds of iterations; a spike is a red flag.
- `raw_reward`: trending up with healthy variance; saturating at one value suggests collapse.
- `kl_loss` (only with `--use-kl-loss`): bounded, drifting up; a sudden jump means the policy diverged from the reference.
- `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff`: stable and much smaller than 1; climbing without bound means train and inference precision drift.

The rest of the table:

- `entropy_loss`: slowly decreasing; falling to about 0 fast means mode collapse.
- `grad_norm`: below `clip_grad` (1.0 by default); repeatedly hitting the clip is a red flag.
- `rollout_time` vs `train_time`: roughly balanced; one far larger means a resource imbalance.
- `train/pg_clipfrac`, the fraction of tokens whose PPO ratio was clipped: below 0.2 is healthy; above 0.5 the policy is moving fast, so drop the learning rate.

One rename to know: `rollout/raw_reward` is now the mean reward **before** dynamic-sampling filters, including the groups they drop. Older Miles logged the retained-batch mean under that name; it is now `rollout/raw_reward_filtered`, so dashboards and alerts built on the old meaning should switch.

blocks.title: Eight rollouts, FP8 rollout switched on at step 5 (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Steps 1 to 4 serve BF16 weights. Every metric sits in the table's healthy range: diff about 0.010, grad_norm under 1.0, clipfrac under 0.2, reward rising.
Run A: at step 5 rollout switches to FP8 and the diff jumps to about 0.035, then holds. A jump and plateau is the expected cost of quantized rollout, not a fault.
The size of that jump matches a real Miles check: a 5-layer GLM-5.2 LoRA validation measured 0.0104 with BF16 rollout and 0.0347 with FP8 rollout. Values differ per model and setup.
Run B: the same switch, but the diff keeps climbing, grad_norm reaches the 1.0 clip, clipfrac nears 0.5 and reward falls. That is the table's precision-drift red flag.
Run B's fix is on the fidelity side, not the learning rate: check that rollout and trainer quantize the same way (lesson 7), add R3 on an MoE (lesson 6) and TIS (lesson 4).

blocks.question: You set `--lr 3e-6` with `--extra-args`, and a colleague later edits the recipe's optimizer block to `--lr 5e-7`. Which learning rate does the next launch use?
options: 5e-7, because the recipe is the canonical home of hyperparameters
Miles aborts because --lr is given twice
The mean of the two values
3e-6, because --extra-args is appended after every recipe block and the later flag wins
blocks.explain: Editing the script changes the earlier occurrence, but --extra-args still lands last on the train.py command line, and the last occurrence of a store flag wins. Repeated flags are not an error. If you want the edited value to take effect, drop the override.

blocks.question: A run shows train/pg_clipfrac at 0.55 for several rollouts, grad_norm around 0.9 and train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff steady at 0.012. What does Miles's monitoring table suggest?
options: The policy is moving too fast per step: lower the learning rate
Precision drift: switch rollout back to BF16
Rollout is the bottleneck: add engines
Mode collapse: raise the entropy coefficient
blocks.explain: Clipfrac above 0.5 means most tokens hit the PPO clip, which the table reads as the policy moving fast, fixed by dropping the learning rate. The logprob diff is small and stable, so precision drift is not indicated, and nothing here measures rollout time or entropy.

blocks.md: A Miles launch script is the recipe of record: read its options table and `EXEC:` lines to know what ran, override with `--extra-args` (the last flag wins), and keep lasting changes in the script. Judge the run against the monitoring table, telling a one-time jump in logprob diff from a climb.

lessons.title: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness

blocks.md:
In a turn-taking schedule, the trainer waits for the slowest trajectory in the batch, and then the engines wait for the optimizer. The Miles docs single out the case where this hurts most: rollout time set by a **long tail of straggler trajectories**, which is typical of long-context, tool-use and agentic workloads.

**Fully async** mode (`train_async.py --fully-async`) splits Miles into two concurrent loops. A background rollout worker keeps generation in flight and puts finished groups into a data buffer. The trainer drains the buffer, runs optimizer steps, and syncs weights back. Generation never stops between steps. With `--fully-async --colocate` the two loops share GPUs and take turns, so generation pauses for each training window, while staleness bookkeeping is unchanged.

blocks.title: Turn-taking vs fully async on four engine slots

scenes.caption: Synchronous: 2 groups of 2 samples per step. The batch waits for the 9-unit straggler, then engines idle while the trainer runs. Step 1 ends at t = 20. Simplified toy with fixed lengths.
Fully async, t = 0 to 7: each finished sample frees its slot (sample granularity). Once 2 slots are free, a new group starts, so g2 and g3 run next to the straggler.
At t = 7 the buffer holds g1 and g2, so the trainer starts its first step without waiting for g0. Its weight update at t = 10 bumps the version to v1.
By t = 17 async has finished 3 steps vs 1 for sync (sync ends step 1 at t = 20). Slot busy time through t = 17: 59 of 68 slot-units (87%) vs 31 of 68 (46%).
The price: g4 started under v0 at t = 8, but the trainer reads it at t = 14, when the version is v2. Its staleness is 2. The weight-update pause is ignored in this toy.

blocks.md: Two details make the engines stay full. First, the in-flight cap: by default the worker keeps `--rollout-batch-size` groups generating, and `--async-max-concurrent-samples` decouples that cap from the batch size. Second, **submission granularity**: under fully async the default is `sample`, so every finished trajectory frees its own slot and a new group goes out once `n_samples_per_prompt` slots are free. The alternative, `group`, holds the slot until the whole group returns, which leaves engines idle behind one slow trajectory.

The **data buffer** sits between the two loops. Its capacity is `floor(factor x rollout_batch_size)` groups with `--async-data-buffer-capacity-factor` defaulting to 2.0; when it is full, the producer blocks until training consumes. Every few steps (`--update-weights-interval`, default 1) the trainer pauses generation to install new weights. The default `--pause-generation-mode retract` sends in-flight requests back to the waiting queue and recomputes their KV cache; `in_place` freezes them on their existing cache; `abort` is rejected under fully async because it would kill them.

Because generation spans weight updates, one group can contain tokens from several weight versions. Miles defines **staleness** pessimistically, so a group is never treated as fresher than its oldest token:

blocks.caption: v of t is the weight version that generated token t, and v current is the latest version when the trainer reads the group. Versions count published rollout weight versions; with --update-weights-interval 1, one version is normally one optimizer step.

blocks.prompt: Aborted groups and groups rejected by the dynamic-sampling filter are discarded when they are put into the buffer. Why can't the staleness filter run at put time too?
blocks.reveal: Staleness keeps growing while a group waits. A group that is 1 version stale when it arrives can be 3 versions stale when the trainer finally reads it, because the trainer keeps publishing new weights meanwhile. Whether a group was aborted, or got identical rewards for every attempt, is fixed when generation ends. So Miles checks those two on `put()` and staleness only on `get()`.

blocks.title: Staleness of each group when the trainer consumed it (toy run)

scenes.caption: Staleness = current version minus the oldest version in the group. Step 0 reads at v0, step 1 at v1, step 2 at v2.
With --max-weight-staleness 1, the get-time filter rejects g4. The unused-samples handler then drops it (default) or recycles its prompt with retry.

blocks.md: What happens to a rejected group is set by `--async-unused-samples-handler`: `drop` (default) discards it, `retry` sends its prompts back to the data source. Groups the dynamic-sampling filter rejects are always dropped, since every attempt scored the same and the group carries no advantage signal. If the defaults are not enough, `--custom-async-data-buffer-path` replaces the whole buffer with your own `DataBuffer` class.

The buffer also tells you where the bottleneck is. Miles logs `rollout/fully_async/queue_size` every step. **Pinned at zero**: rollout cannot keep up, so add rollout capacity; async cannot hide it. **Pinned at capacity**: training is the bottleneck, and `buffer_max_staleness` climbs with it. A rising `stale_groups_filtered` means groups age out faster than the trainer consumes them, which wastes the GPU time that produced them.

Fully async makes training **off-policy**: the trainer learns from groups generated under older weights. The docs recommend staying synchronous while you debug a recipe or validate loss and reward code, where an exact on-policy cadence matters more than throughput.

blocks.question: In a fully async run, queue_size sits at the buffer capacity every step and buffer_max_staleness keeps rising. What is the most direct fix?
options: Add rollout GPUs, because generation is the bottleneck
Give training more capacity (or lower generation concurrency), because the trainer cannot drain the buffer fast enough
Switch submission granularity from sample to group
Raise --async-data-buffer-capacity-factor so more groups fit
blocks.explain: A full buffer means rollout produces faster than training consumes. The docs suggest more training GPUs, lower concurrency, or latency-oriented SGLang settings. A bigger buffer only lets groups grow staler, and more rollout GPUs make the imbalance worse.

blocks.question: An agentic batch has 8 trajectories per group; one takes 40 turns while the rest finish in 3. Which setting keeps engine slots busiest while that trajectory runs?
options: --rollout-submission-granularity group, so the group stays together
--pause-generation-mode abort, to kill stragglers
--update-weights-interval 0
--rollout-submission-granularity sample, so each finished trajectory frees its own slot
blocks.explain: With sample granularity, the seven short trajectories free their slots as soon as they finish, and new groups start in them. With group granularity, all eight slots stay reserved until the 40-turn trajectory returns. Abort mode is rejected under fully async.

lessons.title: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled

blocks.md: RL gradients are taken with respect to the log-probabilities of the tokens the policy sampled. In a conventional multi-turn pipeline, the trainer never sees those tokens. The agent runs inside a **harness**, the program that sends messages to the model, parses its tool calls, runs the tools and appends their results. The trainer sees the harness's *messages*, which went through message parsing, tool execution and chat-template rendering (the chat template is the model-specific format that wraps each message in role markers and special tokens to turn a conversation into one string), and then it re-tokenizes them. The Miles report lists what each stage can do: change tokenization, prune earlier reasoning, or reserialize tool calls. One change is enough for the update to be taken on "a trajectory that never occurred", with no error raised.

blocks.title: Retokenization drift on a tool call (toy vocabulary)

scenes.caption: Turn 1: the policy samples these 6 tokens for the tool call {"x": 1}. SGLang returns their IDs and log-probabilities. Toy vocabulary, for illustration only.
The harness parses the call and re-serializes the arguments as {"x":1}. Re-rendering and re-tokenizing that text gives different tokens: the trainer would score a sequence the policy never sampled.
With TITO the session server keeps the sampled IDs as the authoritative prefix. The trainer gets the exact 6 tokens and their rollout log-probabilities.

blocks.md: **Token-in-token-out (TITO)** removes the round trip by giving tokenization to a **session server** that sits between the agent and the engines. The agent keeps speaking OpenAI-compatible chat (the chat completions request format: a list of messages, each with a role such as user, assistant or tool) and sends its full history every turn. On the first turn the server renders the template into `input_ids`. After each successful completion it checkpoints those prompt IDs with the output IDs and logprobs SGLang returned. On later turns it reuses the deepest applicable checkpoint and tokenizes only the appended suffix, overriding any token fields the agent tries to set.

blocks.title: How the TITO session server assembles a multi-turn sample

scenes.caption: Turn 1: the agent sends ordinary OpenAI-style messages. The server, not the agent, renders the chat template into input_ids.
SGLang returns output token IDs and logprobs (and, when rollout routing replay is on, the experts each token was routed to). The server checkpoints prompt IDs plus output IDs.
Turn 2: the agent resends the full history plus the tool result. The server reuses the deepest matching checkpoint and tokenizes only the new suffix.
Collection: the server assembles one contiguous sequence with rollout logprobs, loss-masking tokens the model did not generate (tool output, template).

blocks.md:
Two session rules exist. **Linear** (v1) lets a request extend only the tail of the history, with a one-turn retry, and yields exactly one training sequence. **Branching** (v2, experimental) stores history as an append-only tree: a request attaches at the deepest checkpoint whose message path prefixes it, any unmatched suffix opens a branch, and each selected leaf becomes a sample. The report notes that branching suits harnesses that fork or compact their context mid-task (compaction replaces earlier turns with a shorter summary so the episode fits in the context window).

Harnesses that do not replay messages verbatim are handled by `--session-message-matcher`: `strict` (default) compares role, content, reasoning content and tool calls; `loose_tool_call` also accepts tool-call arguments with the same JSON content serialized differently; `role_content_only` compares only role and visible text.

`role_content_only` is marked high risk. A tool-calling turn often has empty visible text, so two turns that called different tools can match. The stored prefix then wins, and the trainer keeps a history showing a call the agent never made, silently.

TITO needs the exact template and parsers per model family, so there is **no auto-detection**: you pass `--tito-model` (for example `qwen3`, `glm47`, `kimi26`, `deepseekv4`). Each named family is maintainer-verified by two checks: a CPU check that rendered token sequences stay append-only turn to turn, and a GPU check that the invariant survives real inference with stop tokens and tool-call parsing. Unregistered models use `default`, which is best-effort. The session path does not carry images or video yet, so vision-language models use the lower-level `/generate` endpoint.

Exact tokens remove a *structural* cause of mismatch, not all of it. SGLang and Megatron use different kernels, precisions and batching, so the report notes that even a fully synchronous run assigns slightly different probabilities to the same tokens.

That gap shows up in the per-token **importance ratio**. The trainer wants its gradient averaged under its *own* policy p, but the tokens were drawn from the rollout engine's policy q. Importance sampling, from the course "RL post-training infrastructure at scale", corrects for that: weight each sample by p over q, because the average under q of (p/q) times f equals the sum of q times (p/q) times f, which is the average under p of f. Both sides report log-probabilities, so the ratio is the exponential of their difference:

blocks.caption: When trainer and rollout agree on a token, r is exactly 1. Miles logs the pre-clamp ratio, the clipped fraction and the mean of |r - 1|.

blocks.md: A ratio far from 1 makes a token's weight unreliable, and one huge ratio can dominate the batch's gradient. Miles offers two corrections that cap how much any single token can count. **Truncated importance sampling (TIS)**, switched on with `--use-tis`, damps such tokens: it clamps the ratio to [`--tis-clip-low`, `--tis-clip`], 0 and 2.0 by default, and uses the clamped value as the token's loss weight. **Clip-or-pop** drops them: it is IcePop, shipped as `icepop_function` in Miles's `loss/hub/corrections.py`, selected with `--use-tis` plus `--custom-tis-function-path` pointing at it, and it zeroes the weight outside the same interval. With the default lower bound 0 it drops only ratios above 2; slime's IcePop example sets `--tis-clip-low 0.5`. Capped weights are no longer unbiased importance sampling; the slime lesson "Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering" states that bias and points to the slime team's guide for its derivation, and Miles inherits the same mechanics.

blocks.title: Importance ratio per token and the two corrections

scenes.caption: Raw ratio r = exp(trainer logprob minus rollout logprob) for five toy tokens: 1.105, 0.951, 2.460, 1.000, 0.549. Token 3 is an outlier.
TIS clamps r into [0, 2] and uses it as the token's loss weight. Token 3 is damped to 2.0; the rest pass through unchanged.
Clip-or-pop sets the weight to 0 for any token outside [0, 2], exactly like a loss mask. Token 3 is dropped instead of damped.

blocks.md: Which trainer log-probability is the numerator? Not the one carrying gradient. Under `--use-tis` Miles runs the decoupled, three-policy form of PPO from its mismatch-helper docs. The behavior weight divides $\pi_{\text{old}}$, the log-probabilities the trainer recomputes in a forward-only pass before the update, by SGLang's rollout probability, and it is detached so no gradient flows through it. The usual PPO ratio $\pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{old}}$ inside the clipped term still limits the update. `--use-rollout-logprobs` instead uses SGLang's numbers as the old policy and skips the recompute (Miles refuses it together with `--use-tis`), and `--get-mismatch-metrics` logs the gap without changing the loss.

blocks.caption: In words: each token's PPO loss is multiplied by a stop-gradient weight built from the recomputed old policy over the rollout policy, clamped (TIS) or zeroed outside [L, U] (clip-or-pop). Defaults L = 0, U = 2.

blocks.md: One more source of mismatch is not numerical at all. With top-p or top-k sampling, SGLang draws each token from a truncated, renormalized distribution, so the trainer's full-vocabulary probability is not the probability the token was drawn with, even with identical weights and kernels. **Sampling-support replay** fixes the denominator: SGLang returns, for every generated token, the set of token IDs that survived the sampling filters, and Miles applies that support to the actor's logits before the softmax. The support is fixed rollout data; the logits still come from the actor being trained, so gradients flow.

blocks.caption: S t is the support SGLang kept at step t, z theta the actor's logits, T the temperature. Tool and environment tokens are recorded with a support of one token.

blocks.title: Same logits, two probabilities for the sampled token (toy, top-k 2)

scenes.caption: Full softmax of toy logits 2.0, 1.5, 0.5, 0.0, -1.0: 0.496, 0.301, 0.111, 0.067, 0.025. The trainer computes this distribution by default.
Top-k 2 keeps only 'the' and 'a' and renormalizes: 0.622 and 0.378. The sampler drew 'a' with probability 0.378, not 0.301.
Without replay the ratio is 0.301 / 0.378 = 0.797 for every such token, a mismatch with no kernel noise at all. Replaying the support makes both sides score 0.378.

blocks.question: A harness re-serializes tool-call arguments (same JSON object, different whitespace) on every turn. Under the strict matcher, a linear session keeps rolling back. What is the narrowest fix the docs offer?
options: --session-message-matcher loose_tool_call
--session-message-matcher role_content_only
Pass --apply-chat-template so the harness renders the prompt
Set input_ids yourself in each request

The docs say not to apply the chat template manually or set TITO control fields like input_ids.

blocks.question: A token has rollout logprob -2.30 and trainer logprob -1.40, so r is about 2.46. What weight does it get under TIS with the default interval, and under clip-or-pop?
options: TIS 2.46, clip-or-pop 2.0
TIS 1.0, clip-or-pop 0
TIS 2.0, clip-or-pop 0
TIS 0, clip-or-pop 2.0
blocks.explain: TIS clamps r to [0, 2] and keeps the clamped value, so the token is damped to 2.0. Clip-or-pop zeroes the weight of any token outside the interval, so it is dropped. Tokens inside the interval keep their unclipped r under both.

blocks.question: A run sets --rollout-top-p 0.95 and --rollout-top-k 64, so sampling-support replay is on. It also wants a reference-model KL loss and on-policy distillation. What does Miles do?
options: Runs, but computes KL over the support only
Runs, and silently turns replay off for KL tokens
Refuses to start: replay exposes only the support-normalized score, and KL and OPD need a full-vocabulary score
Refuses because top-p needs top-k left at its default
blocks.explain: The replay docs list this as the current objective limitation: the loss interface carries only the support-normalized actor score, so Miles rejects --use-kl-loss, a nonzero --kl-coef and --use-opd with replay. A finite top-p actually requires a positive top-k, so the run's top-k setting is correct.

lessons.title: Connecting an environment: rollout, generate and agent functions

blocks.md:
Suppose you want to train on Terminal-Bench tasks. Each task needs a fresh container, an agent that runs shell commands for dozens of turns, and a test script that grades the end state. Where does that code plug into Miles?

The slime lesson "Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions" showed two hooks you can replace: a custom generate function for one sample and a custom rollout function for the whole loop. Miles keeps both and nests a third, innermost one inside the generate step: the **agent function**, which only runs the agent and environment loop while the TITO session server from lesson 4 records every token.

The three layers, innermost first:

- `--custom-agent-function-path`: an async function `run_agent(base_url, prompt, request_kwargs, metadata)` that talks OpenAI-style chat to `base_url` (already scoped to one session). It is enabled by setting `--custom-generate-function-path miles.rollout.generate_hub.agentic_tool_call.generate` and `--use-session-server`. A returned dict is merged into each output sample's metadata, which is how an environment's grade reaches the reward hook.
- `--custom-generate-function-path`: one sample's generation, `custom_generate(args, sample, sampling_params)`.
- `--rollout-function-path`: the whole rollout loop. The docs reserve it for fundamentally different flows such as multi-agent co-evolution.

Each layer wraps the one inside it, so replacing an outer layer also takes over everything the inner ones did.

blocks.title: Which responsibilities each kind of connector takes over

nodes.label:
Reward pathway
RM hooks, group rewards

scenes.caption: Agent-function connectors (Harbor, NeMo Gym, OpenEnv) take over only the agent and environment loop. Miles still records tokens through the session server, scores, batches and trains.
Generate-function connectors (HUD, Strands Agents, tau-bench) also take over recording, typically by speaking SGLang's native /generate with token IDs in and out instead of the session chat endpoint.
A rollout-function connector (Verifiers) takes over everything above the engines: its own taskset, grouping and filtering, rewards including group rewards, and recording.
Never replaced by a connector: the model, engines and weight updates, advantages and the optimizer. They always stay in Miles.

blocks.md: Two footnotes from the environments page matter in practice. An environment may grade an episode itself (Harbor and tau-bench do), but the score still enters training through Miles's `Sample.reward` and reward hooks, and group-level reward handling stays in Miles. And computer-use agents observe screenshots, which the session server does not carry yet, so the HUD connector records its own per-turn token IDs and log-probabilities and stitches them into one training sequence at the generate layer. Every connector and sandbox integration is marked experimental.

**Sandbox providers** are a separate axis: they provision the task containers *inside* a connector rather than occupying a layer. The docs list AgentENV, Daytona, E2B, Modal and Novita, with a matrix of which connector each has run a real rollout with. Each takes its credential from an environment variable or a key file; on a multi-host cluster the file must be readable where the rollout workers run, because the launcher passes the file's path, never its contents. Provider quirks are real constraints: Daytona accounts carry a total-disk quota across concurrent sandboxes, and E2B builds templates as a non-root user, so a task Dockerfile whose RUN steps need root fails there.

Rewards plug in the same way as in slime. `--custom-rm-path` names `async def custom_rm(args, sample) -> float`; with `--group-rm` a batched version scores a whole group at once. Built-in `--rm-type` values include `math`, `dapo`, `deepscaler`, `f1`, `gpqa`, `ifbench` and `remote_rm`, and a `boxed_` prefix extracts a boxed answer first. A data source can also set `Sample.reward_spec` to choose a grader per sample. `--eval-function-path` takes the rollout-function signature and defaults to the configured rollout function.

scenes.caption: The agentic generate function opens a TITO session and calls the agent function, which posts the task id and the session's OpenAI-style URL to the Harbor agent server.
Turn 1: the agent inside Harbor sends ordinary chat messages. The session server renders the template, SGLang returns token IDs and log-probabilities, and the server checkpoints them.
Harbor runs the command in the sandbox; no model call. Turn 2 resends the full history plus the command output, and the server tokenizes only the new suffix.
Harbor runs the task's test.sh and returns the grade. The agent function returns it as a dict, merged into the sample's metadata, where the reward hook reads it.
Miles collects the session as one contiguous sequence with rollout log-probs. Model tokens get loss mask 1; tool output and template tokens get 0.

blocks.md: The real Harbor integration matches that trace. A Harbor task is four files (`instruction.md`, `Dockerfile`, `test.sh`, `task.toml`), so SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench and custom tasks train through one endpoint. Two modes exist: a separate agent server on a machine with a local Docker daemon (`examples/swe-agent-harbor-docker`), or Harbor in-process with a cloud sandbox provider (`examples/experimental/harbor`). The validated Docker recipe trains GLM-4.7-Flash on one 8-GPU H200 node with 32 trajectories per GRPO step (4 prompts x 8 samples), so the agent server's `--max-concurrent` must be at least 32: one sandbox per trajectory in a rollout step. Timeouts must be ordered: the server's `--agent-timeout` fires first, below the client's `AGENT_TRIAL_TIMEOUT` (default 7200 s).

    await post(f"{base_url}/v1/chat/completions", payload)
    return None   # or a dict, e.g. {"reward": 1.0}, merged into sample metadata

The price: arguments and return values must be picklable, and module-level state lasts one call, so a module-level semaphore limits nothing. Use `rollout_semaphore` from `miles.rollout.agentic.rollout_limits`, or `inline` mode for debugging.

You keep Miles's data source but lose batching

The environments table marks the model, engines, weight updates, advantages and optimizer as staying in Miles for every connector.

Here the client fires first: the trial is recorded as aborted while the agent server keeps running it, holding its sandbox and --max-concurrent slot, and the aborted sample drops its whole group. blocks.md: Pick the innermost layer that fits: an agent function keeps Miles's exact token recording, reward hooks and batching; a generate function takes over recording; a rollout function takes over data, batching and rewards too. Sandbox providers are chosen separately, inside the connector.

lessons.title: MoE routing replay: why experts flip and how R3 pins them

blocks.md: TITO gives the trainer the exact tokens. For a mixture-of-experts model that is still not enough to reproduce the rollout's log-probabilities. Each MoE layer's router scores the experts with a learned linear layer and keeps the top-k (the k experts with the highest scores). The Miles docs point out that, in production, that router runs with non-deterministic kernels (kernels that may add up floating-point partial sums in a different order from run to run, which changes the last bits of the result) and FP8 quantization, so tiny numerical differences flip which experts win, independently at every layer and for every token.

blocks.title: Router probabilities for two tokens over four experts (toy)

scenes.caption: Softmax of toy router logits. The trainer's logits differ from rollout's by at most 0.02 per expert, the kind of gap different kernels and FP8 can produce.
Top-2 routing. Token B picks {E1, E2} on both sides. Token A picks {E0, E2} in rollout but {E0, E3} in the trainer: E2 and E3 were 0.006 apart and swapped.
Without R3 the gradient for token A flows into E3, which never produced the sampled token, while E2, which did, gets no update.
With R3 the trainer replays the recorded rollout routes, {E0, E2} for token A, so both sides use identical expert allocation.

blocks.md: The report spells out the consequence: the update reaches an expert that never contributed to the sampled token, while the expert that did gets nothing. Across layers, tens of thousands of tokens and thousands of steps, the trained policy drifts from the one that generated the data, and since the next batch comes from the drifted policy, the error compounds. It cites Ma et al. (2025), the paper that introduced rollout routing replay, reporting that this routing mismatch can end in catastrophic training collapse.

**Rollout Routing Replay (R3)** treats routing as rollout data. With `--use-rollout-routing-replay`, Miles turns on SGLang's routed-expert return, so each response carries `routed_experts` of shape `(seq_len - 1, num_layers, top_k)` in `int32`: for each token position, the indices of the top_k experts chosen at every layer. There are seq_len minus 1 positions because the last sampled token is only ever an output: it was never fed back through the model, so it has no routing to record. Miles stores it on the sample, and the trainer's `RoutingReplayManager` plugs the recorded routes into the forward pass instead of recomputing them. Because the TITO session server records routed experts alongside token IDs, replay covers whole multi-turn episodes.

blocks.caption: Routing metadata for one 32K-token trajectory, 60 layers, top-8 experts, int32 entries of 4 bytes each: 32,767 positions times 60 layers times 8 experts times 4 bytes. The docs call it roughly 60 MB per sample.

blocks.prompt: Your agentic episodes grow to 128K tokens (131,072) on the same 60-layer, top-8 model. How much routing metadata does each trajectory now carry?
blocks.reveal: $(131072 - 1) \times 60 \times 8 \times 4 = 251{,}656{,}320$ bytes, about 240 MiB per trajectory. The cost is linear in sequence length, which is why the report calls replayed routes "cheap to replay but expensive to carry" and ties them to Miles's memory-saving work.

blocks.md: R3 is a per-recipe choice. It does nothing for a dense model. The docs also say it is not required when the estimator is `reinforce_plus_plus` and `--use-tis` already masks the off-policy term, and the report adds that in async RL, where many other factors cause mismatch, R3 may have limited effect. Several shipped MoE GRPO recipes turn it on (MoE names such as Qwen3-30B-A3B give total and active parameters: 30 billion in all, of which about 3 billion, the A for active, run for each token, because the router picks only a few experts); the GLM-5.2 reference run leaves it off and relies on TIS.

Why can a recipe that uses TIS skip R3? Split the gap. With the same experts chosen, kernel and precision noise moves a token's probability slightly: a **numerical** part that dense models have too. When two experts are nearly tied at the top-k cutoff, the noise flips which one runs and the layer's output jumps: an **expert-selection** part. Ma et al. measured this on Qwen3-30B-A3B under SGLang and Megatron: about 10% of router decisions differed, 94% of tokens saw a different expert in at least one layer, and the estimated train-inference KL was 1.535e-3, against 6.4e-4 for the dense Qwen3-8B. Replaying routes brought the MoE down to 7.5e-4, close to the dense level.

blocks.title: Train-inference KL, x 1e-3 (Ma et al. 2025, Qwen3 models)

scenes.caption: The dense model shows only the numerical part, 0.64. The MoE shows 1.535: the extra 0.895 comes from routing flips. Simplified: treating the two parts as additive is an approximation.
With R3 the MoE falls to 0.75, near the dense level. What remains is the numerical part, which replay cannot remove and TIS or the precision contract must handle.

blocks.md: TIS does not know why a ratio is off. It acts on each token's final ratio, so a routing flip that moves a token's probability by more than a factor of 2 upward is clamped (TIS) or dropped (clip-or-pop), whatever caused it. In the same paper, without R3 more than 10% of tokens had a ratio beyond a factor of 2 after 60 steps in one GRPO setting; with R3 that fraction stayed below 1e-4. So the two overlap: TIS limits the damage of extreme tokens, while R3 removes the cause and also sends the gradient to the experts that actually produced each token, which no per-token weight can do. In the paper R3 beat TIS alone, and adding TIS on top of R3 gave no clear gain. The Miles docs pair skipping R3 with `reinforce_plus_plus` plus TIS without giving a further reason.

blocks.question: An MoE run uses TIS with the default interval but no R3. Which effect of a routing flip does TIS NOT undo, even when it catches the token?
options: The token's probability ratio exceeding 2
An outlier token dominating the batch gradient
The token's loss weight being larger than 2
The gradient for that token flowing into an expert that never produced it during rollout
blocks.explain: TIS clamps or drops the token's weight, which bounds its ratio and its share of the gradient. But whatever weight the token keeps, the trainer's forward pass still routed it through its own experts, so the update reaches experts rollout never used. Only replaying the routes fixes that.

blocks.question: Which run gains nothing from --use-rollout-routing-replay?
options: A GRPO run on Qwen3-30B-A3B with FP8 rollout
A multi-turn agentic run on a 744B MoE
A GRPO run on dense Qwen3-4B
A GSPO run on GLM-4.7-Flash
blocks.explain: R3 replays expert routing. A dense model has no router, so there is nothing to record or replay. The other three are MoE models where routing can flip between rollout and training.

lessons.title: Low-precision RL: formats, scales and the precision contract

blocks.md:
Take one block of four weights, 0.2914, -0.0071, 0.1337 and -0.4420, and an activation vector 1.0, 2.0, -1.5, 0.5. Rollout serves the block in FP8 with one scale (largest magnitude divided by 448, E4M3's largest value), so its weights become 0.2841, -0.0069, 0.1263 and -0.4420. A BF16 trainer keeps them in BF16. The dot product comes out -0.1401 in rollout and -0.1446 in the trainer: same weights, two answers, before any kernel noise.

The slime lesson "Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4" showed the rollout-side copy: train in BF16, serve a 128 x 128 block-FP8 checkpoint, re-quantize fresh weights at every sync. The formats themselves (E4M3, E2M1, block and microscaling scales) are recapped briefly below. This lesson is what Miles adds: quantizing the trainer's forward pass the same way.

Low precision is the other big source of rollout and trainer disagreement. The report notes that tensor cores (the matrix-multiply units inside NVIDIA GPUs) roughly double their peak rate each time precision halves, with 8-bit floats on Hopper (the H100 generation) and 4-bit on Blackwell (the B200 and GB300 generation). But if only rollout is quantized, or the two sides quantize differently, the same weights compute different numbers and the gap accumulates layer by layer. Miles's answer is a **precision contract**: rollout and the trainer's forward pass run the same quantization logic, and it is enforced at four stages: checkpoint conversion, trainer forward, SGLang rollout, and the live weight export at each update.

Low-precision formats are named by their bit split: **E4M3** has a sign bit, 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits; **E2M1** has 2 and 1; **UE8M0** is an unsigned 8-bit exponent with no mantissa, so it can only hold a power of two. With so few bits a format spans only a narrow range of magnitudes, so numbers are stored in **blocks** that share one **scale**, kept in a format with more range: each stored value is multiplied by its block's scale to recover the real number. **MXFP8** is the 8-bit member of the Microscaling (MX) formats from the Open Compute Project, and **NVFP4** is NVIDIA's own 4-bit format.

blocks.title: Storage bits per weight value, scales included

scenes.caption: BF16 has no scales. Block FP8 adds one FP32 scale per 16,384 values: 8 + 32/16384 = 8.002 bits.
MXFP8: 8 + 8/32 = 8.25 bits. NVFP4: 4-bit E2M1 plus an 8-bit E4M3 scale per 16 values, 4 + 8/16 = 4.5 bits (the per-tensor FP32 scale is negligible).

blocks.md:
The formats with an end-to-end recipe:

- **Block-wise FP8** (DeepSeek-style 128x128 blocks, FP32 scales): Hopper, Blackwell and AMD MI350X/MI355X; generally available.
- **MXFP8**: 32 consecutive E4M3 values share one UE8M0 scale; used for rollout, forward, and both gradient GEMMs (general matrix multiplies: in the backward pass each linear layer does one for the input gradient and one for the weight gradient); Blackwell only, Beta.
- **NVFP4**: E2M1 values in 16-value blocks with an E4M3 block scale inside an FP32 tensor scale; per-token activation scaling; only the routed experts' FC1 and FC2 GEMMs (the first and second linear layers of each expert's feed-forward network) are quantized, with a BF16 KV cache and a high-precision backward by default; Blackwell only, Beta.

Where does quantization happen in a run? At four stages, and the contract covers all four. **Checkpoint conversion** writes the rollout checkpoint (`tools/convert_hf_to_mxfp8.py`, `convert_hf_to_nvfp4.py`). The **trainer forward** runs the matching low-precision GEMM through Transformer Engine. **SGLang rollout** runs the same format. And the **live weight export** at every update re-quantizes the trainer's freshly updated weights into the rollout's layout, and the requantization can also run on the engines after transfer: Kimi-K2's P2P updates in lesson 8 include about 0.88 s of GPU requantization in SGLang's post-load step. The MXFP8 and NVFP4 recipes share a bit-exact quantizer, so trainer and rollout kernels see identical quantized values. NVFP4 adds two details: activations are scaled per token, so artifacts do not depend on which other requests share a batch, and gate and up projections are quantized together so the fused rollout GEMM uses one outer weight scale.

blocks.title: The four stages a precision contract must cover

nodes.label:
BF16 exceptions
by layer and name

scenes.caption: BF16 train, FP8 serve: conversion, export and rollout quantize, but the trainer's forward runs BF16. Lowest friction, but the two sides compute different numbers.
Unified block FP8, MXFP8 or NVFP4: the trainer forward runs the same quantized GEMM, so all four stages agree.
Some tensors stay BF16: final layers, shared experts, MLA projections whose contraction axis does not fit a 1D block. An exception must be applied at all four stages.
An exception set at only some stages (say, conversion but not the Megatron side) breaks the contract: one side quantizes a tensor the other keeps in BF16.

blocks.md: Not every pairing works. Same format on both sides is allowed; so is a BF16 trainer with block-FP8 or MXFP8 rollout. NVFP4 rollout pairs only with an NVFP4 trainer, because NVFP4 needs every stage that touches the weights to quantize them. A newer special case: DeepSeek-V4 ships its routed experts in MXFP4, and Miles serves them as MXFP4 weights times MXFP8 activations with an MXFP8 trainer, optionally with MXFP4 quantization-aware training of those experts. Trainer flags: `--transformer-impl transformer_engine --bf16` plus `--fp8-format e4m3 --fp8-recipe blockwise` (or `mxfp8`), or `--fp4-format e2m1 --fp4-recipe nvfp4` for NVFP4. MXFP8 and NVFP4 need Blackwell; A100 runs BF16 only. NVFP4 has one optional refinement, four-over-six (Cook et al. 2025), shown below: because it changes the quantized values, it must be on in both Transformer Engine (trainer) and FlashInfer (SGLang).

blocks.title: Quantizing one block to FP4 E2M1, two ways (simplified)

scenes.caption: A block of 8 values (real NVFP4 blocks hold 16). E2M1 can only represent magnitudes 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6, times the block scale.
Standard scaling maps the largest magnitude, 3.0, to 6: scale 0.5. Values 2.2, 2.6 and -2.3 land far from their originals. Mean squared error 0.0403.
Mapping 3.0 to 4 instead gives scale 0.75 and a finer grid where these values sit. MSE 0.0188. Four-over-six tries both per block and keeps the lower error. Scale rounding to E4M3 ignored.

blocks.md: "BF16 train, FP8 serve" is the lowest-friction mode, but it is not a contract: the docs say there is precision drift between the two paths, and on MoE workloads you should pair it with R3 and optionally TIS.

**INT4 QAT** (quantization-aware training) is the other option. SGLang serves routed-expert weights from a packed W4A16 checkpoint: 4-bit weights, 16-bit activations. The trainer keeps its BF16 parameters and, right before each grouped-expert GEMM, rounds every weight group onto the INT4 grid and back (fake quantization); backward uses a straight-through estimator, so the gradient updates the original weight as if no rounding happened. Example: the group 0.31, -0.12, 0.05, 0.44, -0.27, 0.02, 0.19, -0.40 gets scale 0.44 / 7 = 0.0629 and codes 5, -2, 1, 7, -4, 0, 3, -6, so the forward sees 0.3143, -0.1257, 0.0629, 0.44, -0.2514, 0, 0.1886, -0.3771.

blocks.caption: Symmetric INT4 fake quantization from the Miles INT4 QAT page. The trainer's group size comes from OPEN_TRAINING_INT4_GROUP_SIZE and the checkpoint's from its config; they are set separately, and matching them does not by itself make the two paths bitwise identical.

blocks.md: One more Miles option attacks a quieter problem. Training keeps FP32 master weights and a BF16 working copy, which is also what rollout gets. At RL learning rates many updates are smaller than half a BF16 spacing (0.0078 just above 1.0), so rounding the master to the nearest BF16 value leaves the working weight unchanged, step after step. Setting `OPEN_TRAINING_BF16_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_FLAG=1` in the trainer environment rounds up or down at random, with probability proportional to distance, so the BF16 copy tracks the master on average. Miles seeds the random bits from the seed, step and shard, so resumed runs rebuild the same weights.

blocks.code:
import torch
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
n, update = 100_000, 1e-6          # 100k weights, each step adds 1e-6 to the FP32 master
master = torch.ones(n, dtype=torch.float32)

def to_bf16_stochastic(x):          # add random low bits, then keep the top 16 bits
    noise = torch.randint(0, 1 << 16, x.shape, generator=g, dtype=torch.int32)
    return ((x.view(torch.int32) + noise) & ~0xFFFF).view(torch.float32)

for s in range(1, 2001):
    master += update
    if s in (1, 1000, 2000):
        print(f"step {s:4d}: master {master[0].item():.6f} | nearest "
              f"{master.bfloat16().float().mean().item():.6f} | stochastic "
              f"{to_bf16_stochastic(master.clone()).mean().item():.6f}")

# step    1: master 1.000001 | nearest 1.000000 | stochastic 1.000001
# step 1000: master 1.000954 | nearest 1.000000 | stochastic 1.000968
# step 2000: master 1.001907 | nearest 1.000000 | stochastic 1.001915
blocks.caption: Run on CPU (torch, 2 threads). After 2000 steps round-to-nearest has not moved a single weight; the stochastic copy's mean follows the master. Miles's own kernel uses Transformer Engine's Philox generator.

blocks.md: How do you know the contract holds? Miles verifies its recipes by comparing the log-probabilities SGLang and Megatron assign to the same sampled tokens, logged as `train/train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff`; the train-infer mismatch helper's `--get-mismatch-metrics` logs it without changing the loss. Numbers are configuration-specific, not thresholds. On a 5-layer GLM-5.2 LoRA check the docs report 0.0104 with BF16 rollout and 0.0347 with FP8 rollout; a historical full-744B LoRA run with FP8 rollout measured 0.0196 (the lesson 9 case study, a different full-parameter run, averaged 0.0369). BF16 is still the right choice for dense models below about 30B, on A100 or AMD MI300X, and while bringing up a new architecture.

TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

blocks.question: You serve a MoE with NVFP4 on B200s to speed up rollout but keep the trainer in BF16 to save engineering time. What do the Miles docs say?
options: Supported; add R3 to cover the drift
Supported only with --use-tis
Supported only on Hopper
Unsupported: NVFP4 rollout needs an NVFP4 trainer forward
blocks.explain: The compatibility table allows BF16 training with BF16, FP8 block-wise or MXFP8 rollout, but NVFP4 rollout pairs only with NVFP4 training. The report explains that NVFP4 requires every stage that touches the weights to quantize them.

blocks.question: An RL run trains in BF16 with a learning rate small enough that most updates are below half a BF16 spacing. Rollout gets the BF16 copy. What happens without stochastic rounding?
options: Many BF16 weights never change, so rollout keeps sampling an older policy than the FP32 masters describe
The FP32 masters stop updating
The optimizer diverges because updates are too small
Nothing: rollout reads the FP32 masters directly
blocks.explain: The masters accumulate every small update, but rounding them to the nearest BF16 value snaps back to the old one until the accumulated change crosses half a spacing. Rollout and training both use the rounded weights, so the policy that actually runs lags the optimizer. Stochastic rounding makes the BF16 copy move by the right amount on average.

lessons.title: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines

blocks.md: After every training step (by default) the trainer must hand the rollout engines new weights. When trainer and engines sit on separate GPUs, this transfer can dominate the step: the report notes that a full NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) broadcast of Kimi K2, Moonshot AI's 1-trillion-parameter MoE, takes almost a minute. Miles offers three transports behind one contract, chosen with `--update-weight-transfer-mode`: `broadcast` (default), `p2p`, and `disk-delta`. `p2p` is peer-to-peer: each trainer rank writes its shard straight into the GPU memory of the rollout ranks that need it, using RDMA (remote direct memory access), where the network card copies data into another machine's registered memory without that machine's CPU or operating system handling each message. The flag also accepts `broadcast_packed`, a broadcast variant that packs each bucket into one byte buffer.

Broadcast and P2P share one preparation pipeline in the Megatron backend. Within each pipeline-parallel stage, tensor-parallel shards are all-gathered, converted to the Hugging Face names SGLang expects, and appended to a buffer (`--update-weight-buffer-size`, 512 MiB, 536,870,912 bytes, by default). A full buffer is flushed as one bucket, so the engines are called once per bucket instead of once per tensor. Routed experts use a separate pass whose expert-parallel gather is deferred to flush time, so the threshold is multiplied by the EP degree to keep the flushed bucket near the target size.

blocks.title: Broadcast vs P2P weight transfer (simplified, EP = 4 on rollout)

scenes.caption: Both modes first all-gather TP shards and convert to Hugging Face names, filling 512 MiB buckets. Here, after gathering, all four train ranks hold the same weights.
Broadcast (default): one sender pushes each bucket over NCCL to every rollout rank, even shards that rank does not need. Each rank receives all experts.
P2P: each sender RDMA-writes only the shard its assigned rollout rank loads, straight into that rank's memory. 4 senders in parallel, each rank gets 1/4 of the experts.

blocks.md: P2P adds three pieces. A **transfer plan** maps training ranks to rollout ranks, giving every sender at least one target so all send in parallel. A **model replica** of each target's layout is built from SGLang's own code with no parameter storage, so running SGLang's weight loaders reshapes gathered weights into the exact bytes that rank expects; the trainer never reimplements SGLang's sharding rules. **Pinned transfer buffers** are registered for RDMA once and double-buffered, so the next group loads while the previous writes are in flight. The report's rule of thumb: with $M$ senders at pipeline depth $p$ and target expert-parallel degree $e$, P2P draws on about $M/p$ times more send bandwidth and each target receives about $e$ times less data. The reasoning: broadcast sends from one source rank per pipeline stage, so $p$ senders work at once, while P2P lets all $M$ send, $M/p$ times as many. And a rollout rank whose experts are spread over $e$ GPUs holds only $1/e$ of them, so it needs only that share instead of every expert.

blocks.prompt: Before looking at the measurements: on a single node with 4 training and 4 rollout GPUs, will P2P beat broadcast?
blocks.reveal: No. On one node P2P was **68.6% slower** (4.23 s vs 2.51 s for GLM-4.7-Flash). A single node gives the senders no extra aggregate bandwidth, and P2P still pays for host-side re-sharding and pinned-memory staging every update. That is why broadcast stays the default and the report recommends P2P only when both fleets span more than one node.
