P2P RDMA: 4.23, 2.16, 2.64, 3.16, 8.48, 7.23 s. Changes: +68.6%, -19.1%, -47.3%, -70.6%, -85.5%, -86.4%. Kimi-K2 includes about 0.88 s of GPU requantization of the fresh weights into the rollout's quantized layout (lesson 7).

blocks.md: The third transport, **disk-delta**, needs no shared fabric at all, only a shared filesystem. Each rollout host starts from the same base checkpoint; at each update the trainer publishes only the changed bytes, each host patches its local copy, and Miles pauses generation only to reload. Two encodings exist. **XOR** (default) is compact but is an involution: applying it twice restores the old weights, so it must be applied exactly once against its declared base. **Overwrite** stores positions and new values and is idempotent: applying it a second time changes nothing. Miles checksums each resulting tensor and stops the update before any engine reloads if the base or a checksum does not match.

How do you know the engines got the right bytes? `--check-weight-update-equal` fills the engines' tensors with random values *before* the first update and then compares each one against the trainer's. Any tensor the transport failed to write still holds noise, so a silent omission cannot pass. It is meant for validation runs, not every step.

Long runs also lose engines. With `--use-fault-tolerance`, a health-monitor thread per server group pings each SGLang engine, kills the ones that do not answer, and the trainer restarts them before its next weight update. Rollout fault tolerance requires a partial-target weight update, one that writes to each engine separately rather than through one collective group that every engine must join, which today means `--update-weight-transfer-mode p2p` without `--colocate`; P2P keeps its per-layout model replicas, so a reconnect rebuilds only the connections to the new engine.

blocks.title: Recovering a dead SGLang engine without restarting the run

scenes.caption: Every --rollout-health-check-interval seconds (default 30) the monitor calls health_generate on each engine.
The engine hangs. After --rollout-health-check-timeout (default 30 s) the call raises, and the monitor shuts it down, ray.kill()s it and sets its slot to None.
Before its next weight update the trainer calls recover_updatable_engines: monitoring pauses and the server restarts engines in empty slots.
The weight updater connects to the new engine and the next transfer proceeds normally; the run never restarts.

blocks.md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

blocks.question: A disk-delta update in XOR encoding is accidentally applied twice to the same rollout host. What state does the host end up in?
options: The new weights, because XOR is idempotent
The previous weights, because XOR applied twice cancels itself
A corrupted mix, detected only at the next step
The base checkpoint from step 0
blocks.explain: XOR is an involution: (w XOR d) XOR d = w. So a second application silently undoes the update. That is why the report says an XOR delta must be applied exactly once and against its declared base, and why the overwrite encoding exists for retry-prone setups.

blocks.question: You train GLM-5 (744B) with 16 nodes per side and weight sync is eating about a minute per step. Which change matches the measurements in the docs?
options: Keep broadcast but double --update-weight-buffer-size; P2P only helps dense models
Use --colocate; the transfer then becomes P2P automatically
Switch to --update-weight-transfer-mode p2p; it cut GLM-5 updates from 58.3 s to 8.5 s
Switch to P2P only if you run on a single node
blocks.explain: The measured GLM-5 update fell 85.5% with P2P at 16 nodes per side. P2P's advantage grows with fleet width and is largest on MoE models, where expert parallelism cuts per-target data. On a single node it was slower. Colocated runs hand weights over locally, with no transport.

lessons.title: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run

blocks.md: **On-policy distillation (OPD)** trains a student on its *own* trajectories while a stronger teacher supplies the signal. Conventional distillation trains on text the teacher wrote, which the student would rarely produce. OPD lets the student generate, then asks the teacher how likely each sampled token is. The per-token signal is the difference of the two log-probabilities of the sampled token, a one-sample estimate of the reverse KL divergence at that position. KL divergence measures how far one distribution is from another and is 0 only when they match. The *reverse* direction, KL of the student from the teacher, is the average of log p_student minus log p_teacher over tokens the **student** samples, so the token it actually sampled gives an unbiased one-sample estimate; the forward direction would average over the teacher's samples instead.

blocks.caption: In words: token t's new advantage is its advantage A t minus lambda times (student log-probability minus teacher log-probability). Miles subtracts the signal from the advantage after the chosen estimator runs; the coefficient is --opd-kl-coef (default 1.0).

blocks.title: On-policy distillation on four sampled tokens (toy, A = 1)

scenes.caption: Student probabilities of the tokens it sampled: 0.60, 0.30, 0.90, 0.05.
The teacher scores the same token IDs: 0.30, 0.60, 0.90, 0.20. The signal d = log p_student minus log p_teacher is 0.693, -0.693, 0, -1.386.

Adjusted advantage A minus d: 0.307, 1.693, 1.000, 2.386. Token 1, which the student over-favored, still gets a positive but much smaller push (0.307); tokens the teacher prefers get a bigger one; agreement leaves A unchanged.

blocks.md: Because OPD edits advantages rather than adding a loss term, it composes with GRPO, PPO, REINFORCE++ and GSPO, and a run can keep the task reward or set it to zero and distill alone. OPD is switched on with `--use-opd`, and `--opd-type` (required with it) picks one of two teacher placements. With `sglang`, an external SGLang server scores each finished trajectory during rollout; the teacher may be a different architecture or too large to co-locate, but it must share the student's tokenizer because it scores the student's token IDs, and it supports a top-K variant (estimating the reverse KL over several likely tokens at each position instead of only the sampled one) and per-prompt routing to several teachers. With `megatron`, a second model of the same architecture is loaded beside the student and scored in the training step.

The documented self-distillation run on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B used a teacher improved by five RL steps and a zero task reward. Over five steps, response length on held-out prompts from the DAPO math set fell from 14,070 to 6,132 tokens, a 56% reduction, while accuracy moved from 84.0% to 85.2%. The report is careful: that 1.2-point change is inside the roughly 1.6-point standard error (the spread in measured accuracy expected from sampling alone), so the supported claim is shorter answers with no reliable accuracy change.

**True-on-policy alignment** goes further than TIS: instead of correcting the importance ratio, it makes it exactly 1. Both sides run FlashAttention-3 (the Hopper version of the fused attention kernel) and batch-invariant matmul kernels (whose result for one sequence does not depend on which other sequences share the batch), Megatron swaps fused Transformer Engine kernels (NVIDIA's library of fused, mixed-precision transformer layers) for implementations matching SGLang, both run in deterministic modes, and the rollout engine re-scores finished sequences with a prefill pass (one forward pass over the whole finished sequence). In supported configurations the reported logprob difference is exactly zero. The costs: slower rollout, and current coverage is only dense Qwen3 0.6B and 4B; Miles refuses to start it on other models.

Where does a nonzero gap come from when the weights are identical? Floating-point addition is not associative, and fast matmul kernels choose how to split a long sum (for example how many partial sums over the inner dimension, called split-K) based on the batch shape. The same token, scored inside a decode batch of one size and a training batch of another, is summed in a different order and comes out a few bits different. Batch-invariant kernels fix the order per row, whatever else shares the batch, and true-on-policy alignment pins every remaining operator the same way. Miles inherited this mode from slime, where it was first implemented.

blocks.code:
import torch                       # CPU toy: one token's log prob under two reduction orders
torch.manual_seed(0); d, vocab, tok = 4096, 8192, 17
W = (torch.randn(d, vocab) / d**0.5).bfloat16(); h = torch.randn(1, d).bfloat16()

def logits_split_k(h, W, splits):  # bf16 partial sums, added in order
    parts = [(h[:, c].float() @ W[c].float()).bfloat16()
             for c in torch.chunk(torch.arange(d), splits)]
    out = parts[0].float()
    for p in parts[1:]:
        out = (out + p.float()).bfloat16().float()
    return out

lp = lambda z: torch.log_softmax(z, -1)[0, tok].item()
rollout, trainer = lp(logits_split_k(h, W, 1)), lp(logits_split_k(h, W, 8))
print(f"split 1: {rollout:.6f}  split 8: {trainer:.6f}  diff {abs(rollout-trainer):.2e}")
print(f"both split 8: diff {abs(lp(logits_split_k(h, W, 8)) - trainer):.2e}")

# split 1: -9.716957  split 8: -9.716116  diff 8.41e-04
# both split 8: diff 0.00e+00
blocks.caption: Simplified: real kernels differ in more than split count (tile order, fusions, attention), but the mechanism is the same. Run with torch 2 on CPU.

blocks.title: One token's |log prob gap| between two engines (CPU toy above)

scenes.caption: Rollout sums the 4096-term dot products in one pass, the trainer in 8 chunks. Same weights, same token: the log probs differ by 8.41e-4, an importance ratio of 1.00084.

Fix the reduction order on both sides and the gap is exactly 0. By pinning every operator this way, Miles's documented Qwen3-4B run logs train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff of exactly 0, with slower rollout.

blocks.md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

The report closes with an end-to-end run that uses most of this course at once: **GLM-5.2 744B-A40B** (744 billion parameters, 40 billion active per token) on terminal-bench-2 coding tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark of tasks an agent completes by running commands in a sandboxed terminal), fully async, on 64 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs (Blackwell Ultra) split 32 for rollout and 32 for training.

- Rollout: eight 4-GPU engines serve FP8 weights and an FP8 KV cache with multi-token prediction (extra model layers that guess several next tokens, used as a built-in draft for speculative decoding); the trainer stays BF16 ("BF16 train, FP8 serve").

In that run:

- Training: TP 2, PP 4 and CP 4 multiply to 2 x 4 x 4 = 32, all the training GPUs, which leaves one data-parallel replica; EP 8 regroups those same GPUs for the expert layers rather than multiplying them. With one replica, each rank's optimizer share, about 279 GB, is streamed to node-local disk.
- Batch: 64 trajectories (8 tasks x 8 attempts) for GRPO, up to 128 in flight; sample granularity kept 90 to 100 requests generating and the prefix-cache hit rate (the share of prompt tokens whose KV cache an engine already held from an earlier turn) at 96% thanks to session affinity (sending every turn of an episode to the same engine).
- Correction: TIS on, R3 off; the rollout and trainer logprob divergence averaged 0.0369.
- Speed: median step 263 s over the first 30 measured steps.

Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

blocks.question: You want to distill a large teacher with a different tokenizer into your student using --opd-type sglang. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; the SGLang teacher retokenizes the student's text
The teacher must share the student's tokenizer, because it scores the student's token IDs
Only the megatron mode allows different architectures
The top-K variant is required for different tokenizers
blocks.explain: In SGLang mode the teacher scores the student's sampled token IDs directly, so the IDs must mean the same tokens to both models. A different architecture is fine; a different tokenizer is not. Megatron mode requires the same architecture.

blocks.question: In the GLM-5.2 run, 128 trajectories may be in flight, yet only about 90 to 100 requests generate at once. Why, according to the report?
options: The router drops 28 requests per step for load balancing
Trajectories waiting on a tool call hold their slot without generating
R3 reserves memory for 28 slots
The buffer capacity factor of 2.0 caps generation at 100
blocks.explain: In agentic RL a trajectory spends time waiting for the sandbox to run a command. It still occupies one of the 128 in-flight slots, but no tokens are being generated for it, so the count of generating requests stays below the cap.

lessons.title: LoRA RL and the multi-LoRA training service

blocks.md:
Full-parameter RL moves every weight to the rollout engines at every update. For Qwen3-4B that is 4,022,468,096 parameters, 8.04 GB in BF16. A rank-32 LoRA adapter on every attention and MLP projection of the same model has 66,060,288 parameters, 1.64% of it: about 132 MB per update, 61 times less.

LoRA in one sentence: the base weight stays frozen and a low-rank product of two small matrices, A (r x in) and B (out x r), is learned and added to it, so an adapted matrix costs r(in + out) parameters. Miles makes that adapter the unit of work: the trainer updates it, the weight-update path moves it, and SGLang serves the newest copy while the base stays resident on every engine.

blocks.code:
# Qwen3-4B, from its config.json
L, h, inter, nq, nkv, hd, vocab = 36, 2560, 9728, 32, 8, 128, 151936
proj = {"q": (h, nq*hd), "k": (h, nkv*hd), "v": (h, nkv*hd), "o": (nq*hd, h),
        "gate": (h, inter), "up": (h, inter), "down": (inter, h)}
linear = L * sum(i*o for i, o in proj.values())
norms = L * (2*h + 2*hd) + h        # layer norms, q/k norms, final norm
total = linear + vocab*h + norms    # tied embeddings counted once
r = 32
lora = L * sum(r*(i + o) for i, o in proj.values())
print(f"model {total:,} params, {2*total:,} bf16 bytes")
print(f"adapter {lora:,} params, {2*lora:,} bytes, {lora/total:.2%}")
print(f"full sync / adapter sync = {total/lora:.0f}x")

# model 4,022,468,096 params, 8,044,936,192 bf16 bytes
# adapter 66,060,288 params, 132,120,576 bytes, 1.64%
# full sync / adapter sync = 61x
blocks.caption: The model total matches the 8,044,936,192-byte total_size in Qwen3-4B's safetensors index exactly. Adapter bytes assume 2 bytes per value.

blocks.md: Miles trains the adapter in Megatron, either through Megatron-Bridge's PEFT (`--megatron-to-hf-mode bridge`) or Miles's native raw-mode plugin, or in torchtitan; FSDP does not implement LoRA training. At each weight-update boundary (every rollout by default, `--update-weights-interval`) Miles exports only the LoRA tensors, with no merge into the base: colocated jobs hand them over through local tensor IPC, disaggregated jobs broadcast them over NCCL (`--update-weight-transfer-mode broadcast`). P2P and disk-delta do not carry adapters. Rollout requests pick the live adapter by name with `lora_path`, and the session server attaches `lora_path=miles_lora` to every agentic turn, or multi-turn episodes would keep sampling the frozen base.

scenes.caption: The trainer holds the frozen base once and updates only the adapter matrices, so optimizer state shrinks to the adapter's parameters.
Colocated: trainer and engine share a GPU, so adapter tensors pass through inter-process communication and nothing crosses the network.
Disaggregated: the same adapter tensors are broadcast over NCCL to remote engines. For Qwen3-4B rank 32 that is about 132 MB instead of 8.04 GB.
Requests name the adapter. The base is never re-sent, so an engine may even serve an FP8 base while the adapter stays unquantized.

blocks.md: Whether a model supports LoRA is a **three-way contract**, not an allowlist: Megatron-Bridge (or a model-specific provider) must build and wrap the training model, Miles must map and export the selected module names, and SGLang must allocate and apply the same adapter modules. A checkpoint whose names look familiar can still fail on its expert, linear-attention or model-specific projections, so start from a validated recipe. The quick-start flags: `--lora-rank 32 --lora-alpha 32 --lora-dropout 0.0 --target-modules all-linear --megatron-to-hf-mode bridge`. Rank 0, the default, disables LoRA; recipes use alpha equal to rank or twice it, and `--check-lora-weight-equal` verifies every synced adapter tensor with SHA-256.

**Multi-LoRA** turns a Miles deployment into a training service. Many clients each fine-tune their own adapter on one frozen base through the [Tinker](https://thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/) API, using the official `tinker` SDK. The client owns the loop: data, sampling, rewards and the schedule of `forward_backward` and `optim_step` calls. Miles owns the GPUs. `create_model` gives each client one of `--multi-lora-n-adapters` slots, each up to `--lora-rank`. Each model has its own command queue; the scheduler packs datums (Tinker's name for one training example) from every model running the same operation and loss into one trainer forward pass, up to a token budget, routing each datum to its own slot. Gradients accumulate per adapter until that client calls `optim_step`, each adapter has its own FP32 optimizer state, and a failure ends training for that model only.

Sampling is **versioned**. `save_weights_for_sampler` writes an immutable adapter snapshot to shared storage; sampling engines load the base once and load an adapter version from disk when a request names it. An in-flight sample against version 1 is never disturbed when version 2 is saved, and since the base is never re-synced, engines may serve a quantized base while the trainer holds BF16. Training and sampling must use separate GPUs: each adapter's gradients stay in GPU buffers between calls, so multi-LoRA rejects `--colocate` and `--offload-train`. It also needs pipeline parallel size 1, and the gateway accepts only the exact `tinker==0.36.0` client.

blocks.title: Two tenants sharing one base model (simplified)

scenes.caption: Both tenants call forward_backward. The scheduler packs their datums into one trainer pass, each routed to its own adapter slot.
A calls optim_step; only A's adapter steps. B's gradients keep accumulating until B decides to step.
A saves for sampling. The gateway writes an immutable snapshot, A version 1, to shared storage.
A samples with version 1. The engine loads that version from storage on demand; the base it holds never changes.
A trains on and saves version 2 while version 1 samples are still running. New requests name v2; in-flight v1 requests finish on the weights they started with.

blocks.question: Why does the multi-LoRA service register every saved adapter as an immutable, versioned name instead of overwriting one adapter slot on the engines?
options: Because SGLang cannot unload adapters once loaded
To save disk space on shared storage
So sampling that started on one version finishes on those exact weights while the tenant keeps training and saving newer versions
Because Tinker clients can only sample once per adapter
blocks.explain: Clients sample asynchronously while they keep training. If a save overwrote the live adapter, an in-flight trajectory could switch weights mid-generation, and its tokens would come from no single policy. Versioned, immutable snapshots keep each sample's behavior policy well defined.

blocks.question: A colleague launches a multi-LoRA gateway with --colocate to save GPUs, and separately asks for P2P transfer in a single-LoRA disaggregated run. What happens?
options: Both work; LoRA sync is transport-agnostic
Multi-LoRA works colocated, but P2P is rejected
Both are rejected only on AMD GPUs
Multi-LoRA rejects --colocate because adapter gradients stay in GPU buffers between calls, and single-LoRA sync uses NCCL broadcast since P2P and disk-delta do not carry adapters
blocks.explain: The multi-LoRA page lists separate training and sampling GPUs as a hard constraint (no --colocate, no --offload-train). The LoRA page says the P2P/RDMA and disk-delta modes do not support LoRA; disaggregated single-LoRA uses --update-weight-transfer-mode broadcast.

blocks.md: In LoRA RL the adapter is what moves: about 1 to 2% of the bytes for a rank-32 all-linear adapter, synced by IPC or NCCL broadcast with no merge. Multi-LoRA extends that to many tenants, with client-owned loops, packed cross-tenant passes and immutable adapter versions for sampling.
